title: Routing boundary design notes — hosted / dedicated / private (sketch)
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes to capture practical differences and trade-offs for tenant routing and isolation across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes. Goal is to bake a set of routing policy primitives we can reuse across control-plane designs and to highlight operational constraints for multi-region failover and data residency.

High-level summary (one-liner):
- Hosted: centralized control plane + global edge routing; logical tenant isolation, multi-tenant runtime pools, best-effort regional affinity, automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
- Dedicated: per-customer reserved pools (soft network isolation), control plane still central for orchestration but routing table includes strong affinity to dedicated capacity; limited cross-tenant fallbacks.
- Private: customer-managed control plane (or private control-plane instances), network isolation by VPC/air-gap, explicit routing boundaries, no automatic cross-tenant fallback unless customer opts in.

Core routing primitives we should standardize:
- RouteKey: tenant_id + model_family + region_hint (string) — primary key for lookup in control-plane route table.
- Policy sets: {latency_slo, cost_tier, region_pref, isolation_level, fallback_strategy}.
- Route targets: {hosted_pool://pool-id, dedicated_cluster://customer-id, private_endpoint://customer-vpc}.
- Fallback chains: ordered list of route targets with a policy for token-level vs request-level fallback.

Isolation boundaries by mode (notes):
- Hosted:
  - Isolation: logical (namespaces + macroscopically shared GPUs). Tenant data in-flight is separated; persistent KV and caches are logically namespaced but share physical caches.
  - Network: public egress via cloud provider; no customer VPC.
  - Control plane: fully managed, global. Routing decisions made at edge control-plane and cached at edge proxies.
  - Trade-offs: easiest for automatic load balancing and global fallbacks; weakest for regulatory isolation.

- Dedicated:
  - Isolation: soft physical isolation — dedicated GPU pools guaranteed to a customer, but management plane still touches multiple dedicated pools.
  - Network: can be placed in tenant VPC or shared VPC with restricted subnets.
  - Control plane: central, but has stronger affinity pins and metadata mapping to dedicated capacity. Control plane can issue per-tenant routing that prefers dedicated clusters.
  - Trade-offs: predictable throughput, still allow controlled fallback to hosted pools (if tenant allows) or to read-only replica for lower-cost long-tail queries.

- Private:
  - Isolation: strong tenant control. Two sub-modes: (1) Redwood-managed private control-plane in customer VPC, or (2) customer-hosted control-plane (air-gapped).
  - Network: customer-managed networking, egress restrictions, possible HSM/KMS in-customer.
  - Control plane: local (per-customer) or federated; routing is owned by customer policy. Redwood's orchestrator only receives telemetry and metadata if configured.
  - Trade-offs: strongest compliance posture, but removes many automated global routing benefits and increases operational complexity for cross-region DR.

Practical routing examples and behavior:
- Tenant A (hosted, US primary) request arrives to edge in us-west: edge lookup by RouteKey picks hosted_pool://pool-23 (us-west). If pool is saturated, fallback_strategy is: try regional hosted_pool://pool-24 (us-east) with cross-region penalty header for caller. Automatic fallback to dedicated clusters not allowed unless tenant has "allow-dedicated-fallback" flag.

- Tenant B (dedicated, EU): control-plane maps tenant to dedicated_cluster://eu-ded-17. Edge will route to nearest gateway that has a healthy connection to eu-ded-17. If eu-ded-17 is unhealthy and tenant allows hosted overflow, control-plane may add hosted_pool://eu-overflow-4 to fallback chain but mark responses with "overflow=true" in trace.

- Tenant C (private, on-prem): RouteKey resolves to private_endpoint://vpc-12-local. Edge proxies in public cloud should not receive tenant data; routing happens via customer VPN/Direct Connect. No automatic routing fallback outside customer network unless explicit peering is configured.

Cache and KV semantics across modes:
- Hosted: shared prefix cache with tenant prefixing. Cache evictions are global; sensitive tenants can opt-out.
- Dedicated: optional per-customer cache instances colocated with the dedicated pool (preferred).
- Private: cache decisions entirely under customer control; Redwood provides optional caching component deployable inside the customer's network.

Control plane design implications:
- Centralized control plane makes policy rollouts and global routing adjustments easy (good for hosted + dedicated mixed fleets).
- For Private we need a federated model: control-plane operator (Redwood) publishes policy primitives, customer control plane consumes and decides local routing. Two-way reconciliation model and signed manifests.
- Critical: certificates and key distribution for route signing; use short-lived certs and rotate via KMS integrations.

Multi-region considerations and failure modes:
- Primary goals: preserve latency SLOs, respect data residency, and avoid cascading failures when a single region is disrupted.
- Region affinity: prefer same-region routing where available; penalty scoring function for cross-region picks (latency + egress cost + regulatory flags).
- Failover patterns per mode:
  - Hosted: automatic edge failover to next available region (configurable priority list).
  - Dedicated: failover to partner dedicated clusters if configured; otherwise optional hosted overflow.
  - Private: failover limited to customer-managed endpoints. Cross-region DR requires customer-run replication and routing rules.

Operational hooks and observability:
- Must emit per-request routing decision metadata: route_key, selected_target, fallback_history, policy_version, decision_timestamp.
- Tracing: correlate edge trace -> control-plane decision id -> runtime instance.
- Cost accounting: mark requests routed to hosted overflow separately for billing.

Unresolved questions / TODOs (working list):
- Policy granularity: do we allow per-route token-level fallback (mid-generation fallback) vs only per-request? Implications for model-state safety. (Action: PLAT-842 to prototype)
- Cache isolation SLAs: what eviction boundaries do compliance customers require? (Ping Legal and Security)
- Private control-plane UX: design signed manifests + reconciliation interval defaults (30s vs 5m). Security review required.
- Network egress accounting and cross-region costs: how to surface to customers when we overflow into other regions?

Quick action items (next week):
- Diego: prototype control-plane route table schema (include policy/version fields) — link to PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1294
- Priya: talk to Security re: cert rotation for federated control-plane (tag PLAT-842)
- Ethan: simulate multi-region failover scenarios for dedicated tenants and measure tail-latency impact.

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight — move final decisions into a formal conops doc once we have experiments/results. This file is an iterative sketch and is intentionally opinionated (helps unblock infra prototypes).

End of notes.
